newsitem.title: POLAND: Warsaw escapes Wroclaw's grim fate in Polish flood.
newsitem.headline: Warsaw escapes Wroclaw's grim fate in Polish flood.

text.p: Flood waters from the swollen Odra River began receding on Monday in the historic Polish city of Wroclaw, but smaller communities downstream were braced for a similar deluge.

With water still covering thousands of square km (miles) of southern Poland, police said the death toll from the week-old catastrophe was estimated at 36, including a German photographer who had gone missing from a boat near Raciborz.
After an urgent cabinet meeting late on Sunday, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz announced a national day of mourning for Friday.
The devastating floods have also caused 31 deaths and huge destruction in the Czech Republic.
Another less dangerous swell of high water, advancing north up the Wisla river, reached Warsaw early on Monday without spilling over river banks or causing serious damage.

Parliament decided to return from recess for a special sitting on Wednesday to amend around 25 laws, including this year's budget, partly to help raise money through borrowing for a rebuilding effort. Cimoszewicz said damage was incalculable.
"It is impossible to rationally estimate the scale...Losses are so vast, no officials can make such estimates," he said.
The prime minister said he would appoint a special official with full powers to draft and implement reconstruction efforts.

Thousands of citizens in Wroclaw, which was part of Germany and known as Breslau before 1945, had laboured over the weekend to save historic areas, a precious library and the zoo from waters that swamped much of the city.
Their sandbag barricades largely succeeded, but many of the main streets remained under up to 1.5 metres (five feet) of water.

Questions arose as to whether the city of 650,000 people could have been spared the huge damage if authorities had overcome resistance by local villagers and blasted gaps in dykes upstream of the city, to free water into the countryside.

Wroclaw council's deputy president, Stanislaw Huskowski, told Gazeta Wyborcza daily that uninsured local villagers, who stopped engineers from blowing the dykes, were desperate because the government had said there would be no compensation.
By the time they were offered full payment for the sacrifice of their homes and farms, it was too late, he said.
He estimated the costs of compensating the farmers would have been 10 times less that those of damage to the city.
"I am 80 percent convinced that this catastrophe would not have happened if dykes above Wroclaw had been blasted in time," he said.
It was one of many reproaches flung at the government, led by ex-communists, which faces a strong challenge from a rightist alliance at general elections due on September 21.
Ministers defended their relief efforts, saying no one could have predicted the huge impact of the flooding.

Where the flooding receded, dozens of towns and hundreds of villages were left strewn with sewage and dead cattle. Officials warned hundreds of thousands of flood victims to clean everything and sterilise drinking water.

Agriculture Minister Jaroslaw Kalinowski told public radio a total of 6,000 square km (2,200 square miles) had been affected and in the southern Opole region, for example, 80 percent of livestock was dead. However, Poland still had enough food and grain.

Cimoszewicz and President Aleksander Kwasniewski went to Germany for a summit that had been designed to pursue closer bilateral ties within a uniting Europe. The two sides will discuss aid efforts, to which Germans are already contributing.
The effects of the flood bit on the Warsaw stock exchange, which fell overall. Trading in seven firms was suspended following their losses due to flood damage.
The Polish zloty also slipped on currency markets but dealers said this was not directly associated with the floods.
